title: Stop Letting the Professor Be the First Person to Find the Flaws
author: howtoteachwithai
source: How to Teach With AI (howtoteachwithai Substack)
summary: Part 4 of a 7-part series on AI-assisted writing instruction introduces two specific AI 'advisor' archetypes: the Red Team Advisor and the Rubric Board Advisor. The Red Team Advisor is configured to systematically attack a student's paper -- finding logical gaps, unstated assumptions, weak evidence, and rhetorical vulnerabilities -- before the professor reads it. The Rubric Board Advisor presents the grading rubric as a panel of evaluators and generates specific feedback for each rubric category. The central pedagogical insight is that professors are typically the first people to identify serious flaws in student writing, which means students have been submitting work they haven't truly stress-tested. Both advisor types can be configured in Claude as project instructions, making them reusable across a semester. The piece includes specific prompt templates and configuration instructions, and argues that making students iterate through AI critique before submission raises the quality floor of submitted work significantly.
points: * The Red Team Advisor configuration inverts the typical feedback loop: instead of the professor discovering flaws, the student's AI advisor attacks the paper before submission, forcing the student to respond to criticism before anyone grades the work. * The Rubric Board Advisor presents grading criteria as a panel of evaluators, generating specific, rubric-anchored feedback that mirrors the professor's grading perspective before the student submits. * Both configurations can be saved as Claude project instructions, making them persistent tools students return to repeatedly across a semester rather than one-time novelties. * The pedagogical argument is about shifting the quality floor: if the professor is currently the first person to identify serious flaws, students are submitting work that has never been stress-tested -- AI review changes that. * The series treats AI advisors not as writing assistants (which produce text) but as critical readers (which evaluate text) -- a distinction that preserves the student's authorial responsibility while improving the quality of feedback available before submission.
quotes: Here is the design problem with traditional writing feedback: the professor is the first person to read the paper critically. Every logical gap, every unsupported claim, every structural weakness -- the professor finds it first. Students have been submitting work that has never been stress-tested by anyone except the person who will grade it.

The Red Team Advisor doesn't help you write. It attacks what you've written. It looks for the weakest point in your argument and pushes on it. It finds the assumption you forgot to justify. It identifies the evidence that doesn't quite support the claim you're hanging on it.

The Rubric Board is five evaluators, each assigned to one dimension of the grading rubric. You submit your draft and each evaluator gives you feedback from their specific angle. You see what a thesis grader would see, what a mechanics grader would see, what an evidence grader would see -- before your professor sees any of it.

These aren't one-time prompts. You save them as Claude project instructions. Every paper your student writes this semester, they bring to the same two advisors. The advisors become familiar. The student starts to anticipate what the Red Team will find. That anticipation is the metacognitive development we're trying to produce.

The goal is not for AI to fix the paper. The goal is for the student to fix the paper after the AI has told them what's broken. The authorial work stays with the student. What changes is how much information they have before they decide the paper is done.
